title: Nervous tissue and the action potential
note: A neuron rests near −70 mV. If graded inputs bring the trigger zone to threshold (about −55 mV), voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ rushes in (depolarization, peaking near +30 mV); then voltage-gated K+ channels let K+ out (repolarization). Action potentials are all-or-none.

read.title: Anatomy of a spike
text: A resting neuron is electrically charged, with the inside about 70 millivolts more negative than the outside. Leak channels and the sodium-potassium pump keep sodium concentrated outside the cell and potassium inside, ready to move.

Incoming signals at the dendrites produce small graded potentials that spread toward the trigger zone at the axon hillock. Excitatory inputs depolarize the membrane; inhibitory inputs hyperpolarize it. They add together, and if the sum lifts the trigger zone to threshold, about −55 mV, voltage-gated sodium channels snap open. Sodium rushes in, and the inside swings positive to about +30 mV.

Two things then end the spike. Sodium channels inactivate, and voltage-gated potassium channels open, letting potassium flow out and returning the membrane toward rest. The potassium channels close a little late, so the membrane briefly dips below −70 mV before settling.

Because every spike reaches the same peak, a neuron cannot signal a stronger stimulus with a bigger spike. It signals with more spikes per second instead. While the sodium channels are inactivated, no new spike can begin, which keeps the impulse moving forward. In myelinated axons, the spike is regenerated only at the nodes of Ranvier, so it jumps from node to node and travels much faster.

q.q: What opens at threshold to start the action potential?
How does a neuron signal a stronger stimulus?
Why does the membrane briefly dip below −70 mV?
o: Potassium channels close a little late
